sources.title: PlayStation cancels live-service shooter Fairgames
sources.text: Haven Games to "shift focus to collaborating with other development teams across PlayStation" PlayStation has cancelled Fairgames, the live-service shooter previously in development at its Montreal-based subsidiary Haven Studios. In a statement to Bloomberg , PlayStation said Haven Studios will "shift focus to collaborating with other development teams across PlayStation Studios, while also exploring new creative opportunities." No jobs have been cut due to the cancellation. According to an email reviewed by Bloomberg, executives Sean Decker and John Doyle informed employees that a recent Fairgames playtest did not meet expectations. "While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set," they said. "Combined with challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game." Haven Studios' debut game was announced in 2023, initially scheduled for release last year, and later delayed to Spring 2026. Jade Raymond founded Haven Studios in 2021, and PlayStation Studios acquired the studio in 2022. Following Raymond's departure in May 2025 , executive producer Marie-Eve Danis and Pierre-François Sapinski were appointed co-studio heads. PlayStation started focusing on the live-service market in 2022 by acquiring Bungie for $3.6 billion . Former Sony Interactive Entertainment head Jim Ryan said the company aimed to launch more than ten live-service games by 2026 . Sony reduced the value of its acquisition by $765 million in the 2025/26 fiscal year after Destiny 2 and Marathon underperformed. Earlier this year, Bungie laid off 292 employees and ended development on Destiny 2. Following the game's final update, Bungie announced plans to reinstate vaulted campaigns , raids, and destinations to restore player trust. One of Sony’s most publicised live-service failures was Concord in 2024 , which was withdrawn from sale two weeks after release. Sony subsequently closed its developer Firewalk Studios , along with Neon Koi. Koi. In 2025, Sony cancelled two unannounced live service titles from Bend Studio and Bluepoint Games. The following year, Sony closed Bluepoint, resulting in 70 job losses . Sony Interactive CEO Hideaki Nishino previously said he wanted to "revitalise" live-service projects through a combination of first- and third-party content following its string of failures. "We believe that live service games are content that attracts users on a global level, so we want to continue to revitalise the market through both first-party and third-party content," Nishino said. "We are not only focusing on promoting new releases, but also considering what we can do with older titles in the medium to long term." He continued: "With live service games, it's important to continuously provide something. The genre itself is relatively new, and I think many people are trying various things, so we also want to continue to take on challenges within that context."

Bungie’s Marathon , which launched this year, has had a rough start , but today the studio showed off some new features coming in a December update , including a new co-op PvE roguelite mode and a PvP deathmatch mode. Sony is also working on a live service Horizon spinoff, but recently rebooted it .

sources.text: Fairgames was revealed in 2023, but nothing more was ever seen of it. A Bloomberg report says Fairgames, a PvP heist shooter announced by Haven Studios and Sony in 2023 , has been cancelled. In something of a surprising twist, a PlayStation rep told the site there will be no layoffs as a result of the cancellation, as Haven will "shift its focus to collaborating with other development teams across PlayStation Studios, while also exploring new creative opportunities." While it was announced three years ago, work on Fairgames appears to have started even further back, in 2021. Just a couple months after her high-profile split with Google Stadia , Assassin's Creed co-creator Jade Raymond announced the formation of Haven Studios , which was "working on an unannounced new IP for PlayStation." In 2022, right around the time former PlayStation boss Jim Ryan was talking about launching 12 live service games by 2025, Sony acquired the studio outright; a year after that, Fairplay was revealed to the world. But things have not gone smoothly since then. Helldivers 2 was a massive hit, but seven of those planned games were cancelled before release . Of the remaining games, one was Marathon , which endures but has not lived up to expectations, and another was Concord , one of the most famously disastrous game launches in years, which was taken offline less than two weeks after it launched, never to return. A live-service spinoff of the Horizon series, Hunters Gathering, was also reportedly rebooted after negative feedback from playtests . A partial accounting of canned multiplayer projects: The Concord catastrophe in particular seemed to shake Sony, which began reversing its live service strategy just a few months later. Fairgames itself looked to be in trouble in 2025 when Raymond departed Haven , reportedly after an external playtest left PlayStation leadership "concerned about how the game was received and its progress." The Bloomberg report says a more recent large-scale playtest produced similar results. "While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set,” PlayStation executives Sean Decker and John Doyle wrote in an email sent to Haven Studios employees. "Combined with challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game." The one bright spot to the cancellation is that no jobs will be cut because of it: A Sony rep told Bloomberg that Haven "will shift its focus to collaborating with other development teams across PlayStation Studios, while also exploring new creative opportunities." sources.title: PlayStation's embattled shooter Fairgames has finally been cancelled, a new report says, as live service push withers away
sources.text: After years of silence, we finally know the fate of PlayStation's embattled live service game Fairgames. The Haven-developed co-op heist shooter has been cancelled, with the silver lining that the studio is not closing down or laying off staff. According to a new Bloomberg report, the decision to cancel Fairgames was made following the results of a recent playtest. Sony told staff on Tuesday of the playtest's poor reception and of its decision to end development. "While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set," executives Sean Decker and John Doyle reportedly wrote in an email to staff. "Combined with challenging market conditions in the PvP shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game." A PlayStation spokesperson later confirmed that developers at Haven will now support other teams within the PlayStation Studios group, as they continue to "explore new creative opportunities". Fairgames was initially announced in 2023 as one of several in-development live service games, as part of an initiative by former PlayStation boss Jim Ryan to create more than a dozen games that generate recurring revenue . Most of those titles were cancelled before they were even revealed, and those that made it out, such as Concord, flopped severely . Even Sony darling Guerrilla Games seemingly can't make it work, with recent reports saying the studio's Horizon Hunters Gathering - initially envisioned as a live service spin on the robo dinosaur series - will now shift into a more traditional co-op structure without live service elements. That's assuming the team can show a revamped version of the game to executives by December. The news of Fairgames' cancellation isn't surprising. The game has had a tumultuous development journey ever since its reveal. Initially set for release in 2025, the game was soon pushed back to 2026 , following the departure of studio founder Jade Raymond . Though Sony later reiterated its commitment to its remaining in-development live service titles , Fairgames was never shown to the public again. That same year, game director Daniel Drapeau left Haven - another key departure suggesting the game had difficulties and might not see release. Throughout that time, Fairgames has reportedly been reworked multiple times, with a plan for it to be re-revealed under a new name. That name is believed to be Break In, linked to a trademark Sony filed in May , but with the project cancelled, we may never know if that was the case.

sources.title: GTA 6 becomes most pre-ordered game on PlayStation and Xbox storefronts
sources.text: Both platforms encourage players to pre-load the game to minimise potential delays and crashes on launch day Grand Theft Auto 6 has become the most pre-ordered game on the PlayStation Store and Microsoft Store. Sensor Tower's GTA 6 sales tracker currently estimates nearly 9.69 million pre-orders worldwide, generating $942 million in revenue. These figures have risen significantly in one week. On November 7, the tracker reported nearly eight million pre-orders and $751 million in revenue. GTA 6 pre-orders have exceeded expectations for Rockstar's parent company Take-Two Interactive . "[We cannot] disclose the numbers, but the point that we're making is our prior expectations obviously were aligned with our guidance, and the pre-orders are far exceeding our original expectations," Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick recently told GamesIndustry.biz . "We're maintaining our guidance, because the release is only 10 days away and we'll know a lot more after the release." In Take-Two's recent Q2 results , Zelnick said the company expects to "deliver a historic year" as a result of GTA 6's launch. Since November 10, GTA 6 has been available to pre-load on PlayStation and Xbox. Both platforms recommend pre-loading to help prevent crashes and delays on launch day, much like what happened with Hollow Knight: Silksong last year . GamesIndustry.biz recently consulted experts on whether GTA 6 could overwhelm internet traffic and if pre-loading will help manage download demand before next week's release. GamesDiscoverCo newsletter author Simon Carless said that "having an extra nine days to gradually send out the bulk of the data to players' computers is vital. There still might be a Day 1 patch/extra download, but if so, it'll be very incremental." Investor and strategic advisor Joost van Dreunen suggested the download bottleneck could still come on launch day, when "tens of millions day-of buyers, not a few hundred thousand" will be downloading the game.

sources.text: On PC, however, GTA 6 remains among the least pre-ordered games of all time because, well, you know. It goes without saying (yet here I am saying it) that Grand Theft Auto 6 is going to be huge. We don't really have a sense as to just how huge at this point: Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick has boasted that GTA 6 preorder numbers are " unprecedented ," but he's refused to provide specifics because "the raw numbers could be potentially misleading." But huge, for sure. Now both Sony and Xbox have joined in the 'gonna be huge' chorus, each of them announcing that preorders for GTA 6 are, definitionally, unprecedented . "Grand Theft Auto 6 is now the most pre-ordered game in the history of PlayStation Store," Sony proclaimed on the PlayStation Blog . "Given this unprecedented demand, we’ve joined with Rockstar Games to allow players to start pre-loading the game nine days early, so they’re ready to play on launch day. We’ve also adopted a rolling midnight launch by country, beginning at 12:00AM NZDT in New Zealand and running across the globe as respective countries hit midnight on November 19." Xbox made a similar announcement on its own website, calling GTA 6 "the most pre-ordered title of all time on the Microsoft Store" and encouraging users to begin preloading as soon as possible because of "the unprecedented demand" for the game. Alongside Xbox Series X/S consoles, Xbox said GTA 6 will also be playable on Xbox One consoles through Xbox Cloud Gaming. That service is also available on PC, but Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Bell confirmed in October that GTA 6 will not be streamable on our platform . But while nobody is serving up specifics on the number of GTA 6 copies sold via preorder, we do have a rough indicator of how much money Take-Two expects to make when it comes out of the gate. The publisher is projecting net bookings of $3.35 to $3.5 billion for its current fiscal quarter, "driven by the groundbreaking release of Grand Theft Auto 6" on November 19. That's roughly double what Take-Two took in during the same quarter in its previous year, when it reported net bookings of $1.76 billion. "The launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 is ten days away and, with pre-orders continuing to reach unprecedented levels, we expect to deliver an historic year for our company," Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick said during yesterday's quarterly financial report. sources.title: GTA 6 rodará no Xbox One por meio do Xbox Cloud Gaming, confirma Microsoft
sources.text: GTA 6 ganha novo teaser e inicia preload após recorde de pré-vendas Se você ainda não garantiu um console de nova geração só para jogar o game mais aguardado de todos os tempos, aqui vai uma boa e inesperada notícia: GTA 6 poderá ser jogado no Xbox One por meio do Xbox Cloud Gaming já no dia 19 de novembro , data de lançamento oficial da sequência. Segundo informações da própria Microsoft, GTA 6 é o título mais pré-encomendado de todos os tempos no Xbox Store, e a empresa recomenda que os jogadores iniciem a pré-instalação o quanto antes. A transmissão pela nuvem começará às 3h da manhã (horário de Brasília) do dia 19 de novembro e permitirá com que donos de Xbox One também tenham acesso ao lançamento. A possibilidade é uma novidade importante, já que o console pertence à geração passada e não consegue executar o jogo nativamente. Nos consoles mais recentes da Microsoft, GTA 6 será executado diretamente no hardware. O Xbox Series X oferecerá a experiência nativa de console com melhor desempenho gráfico, enquanto o Series S será a opção mais acessível para jogar sem depender de streaming. Já no Xbox One, o funcionamento será diferente: o game será executado em servidores da Microsoft e transmitido pela internet por meio do Xbox Cloud Gaming. Nesse formato, o console não precisa processar o jogo, apenas reproduzir a transmissão. Segundo a Microsoft, a versão transmitida pela nuvem utilizará as configurações gráficas do Xbox Series S — e, assim como em todos os consoles, também rodará a 30 FPS . Além disso, a empresa confirmou que jogadores de mercados compatíveis poderão comprar tempo de jogo na nuvem a partir de 11 de novembro, sem precisar de uma assinatura do Game Pass. Se quiser saber quanto custa a hora da nuvem no Game Pass, clique aqui ! Por fim, a companhia afirmou estar animada para levar GTA 6 a mais jogadores no lançamento e também planeja adicionar outros títulos da Rockstar ao serviço, incluindo GTA 5 e Red Dead Redemption 2 . Vale lembrar que o jogo precisa ser adquirido separadamente para acessar a transmissão . Apesar de GTA 6 chegar ao Xbox One por streaming, o jogo infelizmente não poderá ser executado no PS4 . O console da Sony não receberá uma versão nativa do título, e a Rockstar não anunciou suporte ao jogo por meio de serviços de nuvem da PlayStation. A diferença está justamente na forma de funcionamento do Xbox Cloud Gaming. Como o processamento acontece nos servidores da Microsoft, o Xbox One não precisa ter potência suficiente para executar GTA 6 localmente. A PlayStation também oferece streaming de jogos em nuvem por meio dos planos mais completos do PS Plus Premium, mas a disponibilidade varia de acordo com a região e o catálogo de títulos compatíveis. Lembrando que o mesmo nível é chamado de PS Plus Deluxe no Brasil e não possui a disponibilidade de jogos em nuvem. Até o momento, não há confirmação de que GTA 6 será oferecido dessa maneira no serviço. Portanto, entre os consoles da geração passada, apenas o Xbox One terá acesso a GTA 6 por meio de streaming na nuvem. No caso do PS4, os jogadores não poderão aproveitar o lançamento, já que não existe uma versão compatível anunciada para o aparelho. Lembrando que GTA 6 será lançado em 19 de novembro de 2026 para PlayStation 5 e Xbox Series X|S. O título será disponibilizado exclusivamente nos consoles de atual geração inicialmente — mas é bastante provável que uma versão de PC também chegue no primeiro trimestre de 2027, segundo fortes rumores que circularam recentemente . Claro, a pré-venda de GTA 6 também já está disponível , com duas versões do jogo oferecidas nas plataformas — além da versão física sem disco que gerou polêmicas na comunidade . sources.name: Kotaku
sources.title: Grand Theft Auto 5: The Kotaku Re-Review
sources.text: Grand Theft Auto V is the reigning game of all time. One of gamingâs most undeniable cultural exports. An ugly game that casts one unbelievable shadow. A title so massive, itâs become damn near impossible to recreate without burning down your development studio in 2026. Revisiting it in the lead-up to GTA VI âs release later this year has been illuminating in many ways, but the thing Iâm perhaps most struck by about the 2013 hit is how miserable it is. What a fascinating thing to exist in the supposed upper echelon of the gaming pantheon. GTA V is filled with all kinds of missions and objectivesâthe stuff that modern gaming parlance constantly calls “content.” Really, it turns everything into content for you to check off. It’s got big missions and small ones. Simple, boring ones that occasionally lull you to sleep. Distractions like tennis and drag racing. And, on the other end, massive, multi-part setpieces that get the blood pumping a little more efficiently. A gulf separates these sequences. Sometimes I’m little more than a glorified cabbie, at other times a glorified avatar of the âAmerican dreamââa ball of boredom, rage, and discontent at The Way Things Are, armed with a rifle aimed at nothing in particular. Lots of it feels utterly meaningless. Stealing the occasional getaway vehicle and quietly parking it in a nearby lot often counts as a mission, one I hate after doing it multiple times in my ~50 hours revisiting GTA V . Not that its more pulse-pounding action is especially noteworthy either. The game’s crosshair, for example, is wholly unremarkable. It’s just a dot. A dot that, by default, magnetizes to the often nameless nobodies on the other end of your barrel, as if to smooth any friction that could possibly arise in the instant between when you see a foe and when you pull the trigger on your weapon of choice.Â Many other shooters feature different crosshairs depending on the weapon. A grenade launcher might suggest an arc. A sniper rifle, too. A shotgun blast has a wider spread, and a crosshair usually indicates its range. But time and time again, GTA V plays it cool, calm, and detached with its minimalist crosshair. It doesn’t want to bore you with calculating distances and trajectories. It wants you to endlessly put holes in cops, gangsters, hillbillies, rival drug enterprises, federal agents, clowns, aliens, and everything in between, while occasionally piloting several classes of vehicle in increasingly linear scenarios. It doesn’t feel wholly good or bad; it feels likeâ¦nothing.Â Driving around the state of San Andreas and shooting things feels like nothing . A kind of nothing that quicklyâ easily âfills dozens of hours. Like a chore. Maybe that’s the best way to describe GTA V . Well, if itâs going to be such a chore, it feels, at least, like GTA V should aim that tedium at some larger point, shouldn’t it? It kind of does. Each of its endeavors, be it a mundane task, an odd job to rustle up some cash, or a riotous heist spilled out on the streets of not-LA, does in fact feel pointed. Compulsive, even. At least in part because they feel like the backdrop for the gameâs occasionally devastating musings that hit with the force of, well, a getaway vehicle.Â The most consequential series of missions among GTA V ‘s errands is largely divorced from the thrust of its campaign. Itâs got nothing to do with heists and has nothing to do with two-thirds of the gameâs playable trio. Itâs got nothing to do with the city of Los Santos, even. Far up in the middle of Nowhere, Blaine County, is an unsavory duo called the Minute Men, who are on a collision course with a similarly ugly force by the name of Trevor Phillipsâa walking, talking (usually swearing) cancer and truly one of the most detestable protagonists a game has ever saddled a player with.Â The Minute Menâs contributions to GTA V are small but important. Over a triptych of morally repugnant descents into darkness that only Trevor can take on, they try to prove the righteousness of their cause. In a move that felt like a cavity opening in my soul, Trevor rides along with Joe and Josef, two members of the âCivil Border Patrol,â as they chase down and detain Mexican-American citizens across the countryside. Or as one of them says, in his native Russian on American soil, âWell-motivated people, eager to do low-level jobs at any wage to support their families.âÂ These missions are, like the rest of GTA V âs offerings, pretty unremarkable in their construction. You chase after these poor souls in a patrol vehicleâa park rangerâs van with hardly a new splash of paintâtase them (another drab crosshair) and eventually escort them back to the vehicle, where they are subsequently driven to a somewhat ambiguous fate. The whole thing would only run about 15 minutes if the missions were stitched together, and ends with little fanfare. All in all, these excursions with the Civil Border Patrol are a perfect microcosm of what GTA V actually excels at: being a banal cascade of senseless violence and bigotry, bookended by a smug but empty wink. A shockingly vivid reflection of our depravity and our inability to break from it. The mission “Friend Request,” which involves another of the gameâs protagonists, named Michael, breaking into the headquarters of a Facebook analog called Life Invader, is a perfect example. sources.text: Resident Evil Requiem has walked away with the biggest prize of the night at the Golden Joystick Awards 2026 , claiming the title of Ultimate Game of the Year. Competition was fierce for this year's main award, with Resident Evil Requiem coming out at the top of the pile of 12 of this year's biggest games. Those included the massive launches of Crimson Desert and Phantom Blade Zero, blockbuster 007: First Light, surprise hits like Control Resonant and Pragmata, and late additions in the form of Star Wars: Galactic Racer and The Blood of Dawnwalker. Also nominated were Big Walk, Dispatch, Forza Horizon 6, and Pokemon Pokopia. The win capped off a big night for Resident Evil Requiem, which came away from this year's ceremony with four awards; Best Game Trailer for its 'Evil Always Has a Name' promo, Best Lead Performer for Grace Ashcroft actress Angela Sant'Albano, and Console Game of the Year. That might have made it the outright winner, were it not for an astonishing challenge from a very different game - two player-voted and two jury-voted awards for Meccha Chameleon saw the hide-and-seek sensation tie Resi's four wins. But Resident Evil Requiem has still walked away with the biggest prize, and depending on exactly how you count each award, may have pipped Meccha Chameleon to the title, thanks to a Studio of the Year award for Capcom - though with that shared with fellow winners Pragmata and Onimusha: Way of the Sword, perhaps that's a total of just 4.33 awards for Resi. Requiem has been a long-time frontrunner for this year's GOTY conversations. sources.title: Why wasn't GTA 6 at the Golden Joystick Awards?
sources.text: You'll have to wait a little while for Leonidas The Golden Joystick Awards 2026 have drawn to an end, but one of this year's biggest games was entirely absent: GTA 6 . If you were watching the ceremony wondering where Rockstar might have been, the short answer is that GTA 6 was not eligible for entry at this year's show. To be nominated in one of the main categories, a title had to release between November 1, 2025 and September 25, 2026. For the main prize of Ultimate Game of the Year, that window was extended to October 25, and for jury-voted prizes, games are eligible up until the show itself, November 11. That means that games like Dispatch, which launched late last year, or Phantom Blade Zero, which only just released, were eligible to be included in the 2026 show. But GTA 6, which is set to release next week, arrives eight days after the eligibility window closed. It was technically eligible for the title of Most Wanted game, but given that Rockstar won that particular award in 2024 and 2025, and that the wait is so nearly over, GTA 6 wasn't nominated in that category. Adding to the potential confusion is the fact that GTA 6 is eligible for The Game Awards. Those take place on December 10, several weeks after launch, and the fact that they're jury-voted rather than public-voted means that any jurors with review access might have had copies of the game for some time before that show. The rest of the major awards shows - namely the DICE, GDC, and BAFTA ceremonies - take place at the start of 2027, so GTA 6 will likely be a major contender there. GTA 6 will be eligible for the 2027 Golden Joystick Awards, where I'd also expect it to pick up several prizes. That means that it will be able to complete the clean sweep of the Big 5 shows - repeating the feats of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 and Baldur's Gate 3 - but it won't do so in the 2026/7 season. sources.text: Resident Evil Requiem and Meccha Chameleon were the night's other big winners. There was some fun conversation here at PC Gamer recently about the anachronistic name of The Golden Joystick Awards, which are put on by PC Gamer's publisher. Who even uses a joystick anymore? Flight sim diehards, fighting game enthusiasts, and not many others. So why is it called that? Joysticks , really? Simply put, the name reflects the age of the awards, which debuted in 1983, making it the longest-running publicly-voted videogame awards show of all time, according to Wikipedia. Back in those days, joysticks were it, and trust me, they weren't the sweet pieces of hardware we have access to now. But we loved 'em! And we used them to play games like the Golden Joysticks' first-ever game of the year, Jetpac. It was a banger! Here we are, 43 years later, and much has changed: From a tiny ceremony handing out five trophies, the Golden Joysticks have grown to become one of the biggest videogame awards events of the year, watched by millions of people around the world on just about every streaming platform you can name. Yet that name, the Golden Joystick Awards , remains. Frankly, I'm glad about that. A little bit of reliability in this world is good for everyone. Which leads me to the point: The 44 th annual Golden Joystick Awards has now concluded, and the top gong , as my UK compatriots like to say for some reason—the Ultimate Game of the Year award, for the rest of us—has gone to Resident Evil Requiem , Capcom's latest tale of zombie-fueled bad news. Can't really argue with that call: PC Gamer's Elie Gould gave Resident Evil Requiem a whopping 92% score in their review , saying it "feels like you're playing a highlight reel of the best moments in the series." Requiem claimed three other wins on the night: Console Game of the Year, Best Game Trailer, and Best Lead Performer for Angela Sant'Albano's turn as Grace Ashcroft. Crimson Desert won for PC Game of the Year, which surprises me a bit given that it's also on consoles and pretty much the same experience. We liked that one too: Not quite as enthusiastically, but it still earned an enviable 80% review score . "Vast and obtuse in a way that is going to frustrate some and exhilarate others," as reviewer Mollie Taylor put it: "A fascinating journey, even when the destination isn't all that." Multiplayer hide-and-seek game Meccha Chameleon was the night's other big winner, taking home four awards for Best Multiplayer Game, Best Indie Game (self-published), the Steamers' Choice Award, and Developer's Choice Award. Dispatch won twice, for Best Storytelling and Best Soundtrack, and The Witcher also sort of claimed two wins as well: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered took the trophy for Best Remake/Remaster, while The Witcher 4 won for Most Wanted Game. sources.title: The Witcher 3 expansion uses AI to adjust Geralt’s Polish voiceover because the actor suffered a stroke
sources.text: Jacek Rozenek consented to AI being used on his voice lines to make them sound like he used to CD Projekt Red has confirmed that it has used AI to alter some of the voice acting in the upcoming The Witcher 3 expansion, Songs of the Past. Speaking with Game File , CDPR says that it worked with AI company Respeecher to ensure that Geralt’s Polish lines, performed by longtime Geralt actor Jacek Rozenek, sounded similar to the performance he gave in the base game a decade ago. Rozenek gave his consent for the voice lines to be edited by Respeecher. The decision was made due to changes to his voice that came about after he suffered from a stroke in 2019, which left him unable to speak. He returned to voice acting in 2022, but this required hours of training a day. “I was so exhausted after this recording,” says Rozenek, referring to the recording he did for The Witcher 3 ‘s next-gen update in 2022. Therefore, he was supportive of Respeecher’s involvement. “The point is that this voice should be as close as possible to my voice from 12 years ago,” he says. “I have great trustâ¦for the creators of this game.” Following his work on the next-gen update, CDPR called Rozenek back in for the upcoming Witcher 3 expansion, Songs of the Past. When they determined that his voice was too different from how it sounded years prior, the decision was made to work with Respeecher. Rozenek still recorded all of his new lines for Songs of the Past as he would have done before, but the lines were then sent to Respeecher to match them with how he sounded in the base game. The AI tools used to accomplish this were trained on Rozenek’s previous voice work. “We basically delivered to Respeecher all the lines that Jacek recorded for us for The Witcher 3,” localisation producer MikoÅaj Szwed says. “They created an algorithm of his voice, based on his lines.” Szwed also acknowledges the ethical concerns surrounding AI, but argues against the critics in this instance. “I do think this is one of those ways where you can use AI ethically, with consent and also to do something good,” he says. He also stresses that this was only considered because of Rozenek’s health issues. CDPR has used Respeecher’s services previously, as part of Cyberpunk 2077 ‘s Phantom Liberty DLC. That was because the Polish actor for Viktor Vektor, MiÅogost Reczek, had passed away after the base game’s release. Rather than recast him, CDPR opted to create new voice lines with AI , with his family’s consent. This all comes at a time when AI usage in games is under increased scrutiny. Earlier this week, Big Walk developer House House confirmed that it had used AI towards the end of the game’s development to “help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs”.Â This admission came after the jury for The Independent Games Festival said it would not vote for a game that “uses generative AI in any capacity”. Similarly, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 had its Game of the Year award revoked by The Indie Game Awards over its own use of generative art for placeholders, some of which was left in the final game before being patched out.

sources.text: CD Projekt Red Geralt Songs of the Past The Witcher 3 Voice actor Jacek Rozenek plays Geralt of Rivia in the Polish version of The Witcher 3 , but in 2019 he suffered a stroke that made it hard to speak and changed his voice. He added, “I do think this is one of those ways where you can use AI ethically, with consent and also to do something good.” Game File reports that CDPR turned to Ukrainian AI voice cloning firm Respeecher for help, the same company it worked with when one of the voice actors for Cyberpunk 2077 died between the release of the original game release and that of the Phantom Liberty expansion . sources.title: The Witcher 3 uses gen-AI to enhance Geralt's Polish voice following actor's stroke - "I do think this is one of those ways where you can use AI ethically"
sources.text: "I have great trust ... for the creators of this game." CD Projekt Red has revealed that it used - and is using - generative AI technology to treat and alter the voice of the Polish actor who portrayed Geralt of Rivia in upcoming Witcher 3 expansion Songs of the Past . The actor, Jacek Rozenek, has portrayed Geralt of Rivia in all the major Witcher games, meaning his voice has become as synonymous with the role in Poland as Doug Cockle's has for people playing in English. But Rozenek suffered a severe stroke in 2019 that left him temporarily unable to speak, and when he was able to talk and perform again, the tonality and quality of his voice had changed. It's for these reasons that CD Projekt Red - with Rozenek's consent - employed the help of a company called Respeecher to alter the lines he recorded for The Witcher 3 's Songs of the Past expansion using generative-AI technology. As confirmed to Game File , an AI trained on Rozenek's previous Witcher work is retreating his recordings to make them sound more like the Geralt you hear elsewhere in The Witcher 3. "The point is that this voice should be as close as possible to my voice from 12 years ago," Jacek Rozenek explained. "I have great trust ... for the creators of this game." Game File heard both treated and untreated recordings of Rozenek's Songs of the Past work, and reported a "significant" difference between them. Rozenek's untreated voice was apparently "deep and gravelly" and "noticeably rougher than his recordings for the original game". But treated, the voice was "far smoother and sounds younger", and closer to the original Witcher 3 Geralt recordings. This isn't the first time CD Projekt Red has used generative AI for voice recordings in one of its games. The studio worked with Respeecher in 2023 to produce new voiceover lines for Cyberpunk 2077 expansion Phantom Liberty . Viktor Vektor actor Miłogost "Miłek" Reczek passed away in 2021, after the original game was released, and CD Projekt Red didn't want to recast the role. Reczek's sons apparently gave their blessing for their father's voice to be artificially generated. "I do think this is one of those ways where you can use AI ethically with consent and also to do something good," CD Projekt Red localisation producer Mikołaj Szwed told Game File, referring to the Rozenek recordings. "For future projects, when we consider Geralt is becoming older and has a deeper voice, this is not a problem for us at all. It's more about this specific situation here, where we have both the voice from 12 years ago and from now next to each other, which could kind of take people out of the experience and feel that there is this difference." The third Witcher 3 expansion, Songs of the Past, releases at some point next year, an unprecedented 12 years after the original game launched. It adds an entirely new region, Letten, and centres its main story around Geralt's missing bardic bestie Dandelion, whose family lives there. In preparation for the expansion, a remastered version of The Witcher 3 was released a couple of months ago, overhauling the old role-playing adventure and bringing its baseline presentation more in line with what we'd expect from a modern game; it also overhauled some animations and enemy behaviours and reworked skill trees. For that reason, old-gen consoles PS4 and Xbox One won't receive the Songs of the Past expansion, despite The Witcher 3 being available on them.

stories.title: Monster Hunter Outlanders Review
stories.summary: This mobile spin-off maintains the gameplay loop and visuals of its console counterparts, with the caveat of how progress gates push microtransactions.

sources.name: IGN
sources.title: Monster Hunter Outlanders Review
sources.text: If there's a singular idea that defines Monster Hunter, it's the grind. Capcom's mega-hit franchise, ever since its inception on the PSP, has flourished because of how it embraces the very idea of grinding and transforms it into an infectiously fun gameplay loop. Repetition and habit are vital parts of the series, so it makes sense, then, that the mobile game gacha format would eventually come to Monster Hunter, fitting currencies and timed gauges into that collecting and grinding experience. But my biggest surprise with Monster Hunter Outlanders has been how it's a comprehensive, full-fledged Monster Hunter packed onto phones and tablets. While it does eventually get buried under an avalanche of currencies to keep track of and some gacha roadblocks, there's enough meat on the bone here to sustain those hungry for more Monster Hunter or a solid action RPG on mobile. Like most Monster Hunter games, Outlanders follows a group of intrepid explorers from the Adventurer's Guild, this time sent to the uncharted island of Aesolan to investigate a mineral called Radiantate, and how it's influencing various breeds of monsters. After a brief action-packed intro, you're essentially let loose onto the island, free to explore the first environment or tackle the story as you see fit. But also, like most Monster Hunter games, the initial 20 or so hours of Outlanders are extremely guided and layered with seemingly endless tutorials. That's compounded by the nature of being a mobile game, meaning it has to introduce a half-dozen modes, various pull systems, currencies for powering up your Adventurer, and much more. The most succinct way to describe Outlanders is if you took Monster Hunter World , streamlined its combat, and crammed the entire thing into a mobile game. I almost cannot overstate how closely Outlanders resembles World in every way, even right down to the general structure and story. It takes a bit of an interesting approach, filling the story with a cast of characters that doubles as the big gacha pulls, even though you also have your "main" player-created character. While the overall story feels a bit rote and generic, the world of Outlanders itself is still brimming with things to do. While not a traditional open world game, it's in the exact same framework as Monster Hunter World and Wilds , giving you massive zones to explore. In these zones, you can naturally hunt monsters (without kicking off missions), gather resources, engage in little minigames like a rhythmic one where you steal a flying monster's treasure, and undertake any number of sidequests. My biggest surprise with Outlanders is how uncompromising the scope of its world feels, right in line with a big mainline Monster Hunter, supported by the fact that this game looks absolutely stunning, and runs like a dream. On an iPhone 14 Plus I was able to run the game on High settings with a stable 45fps, and almost zero slowdown, even during intense battles. The actual act of exploring the world feels just as entrancing as in major Monster Hunters. Various options for constructing camps and equipment as you explore the world make both traversal and item gathering easier. Camps unlock fast travel points and places to rest, catapults send your adventurer flying on their glider at high speed, and resource collectors constantly soak up those valuable items you need. Combat is still largely about that push-and-pull of timing, knowing when to pivot between offense and defense, and winding up your attacks at just the right time. That timing and weight of battle has always set Monster Hunter apart from other action games, and it's still present here. But where you can see the mobile limitations is in the particulars of combat control and the various, and many systems, used to improve your Adventurer's stats. Essentially, Outlanders is a squad-based Monster Hunter, where you build a party consisting of your main character and characters you pull (multiplayer with other actual players is available, too). But you can also play as each of the gacha characters, who have their own movesets, Ultimates, and abilities. For example, Keres uses dual blades that are actually a set of claws, giving her a completely separate set of skills, including one Wolverine-like drill attack. Meanwhile, Luxheart has a two-handed sword that he can rev up to shoot out fireworks, making each of his attacks like a miniature show. These various characters are actually one of my favorite parts of Outlanders, as their designs dig into a bit of tokusatsu pizazz , leaning into the overall goofiness of Monster Hunter as well. Having distinct movests also goes a long way to breaking up the monotony of repeat hunts and grinding. However, Outlanders overall has fewer weapon types than the last few games as a result, clocking in at eight total weapon types – some notable exclusions being the Hunting Horn and Insect Glaive. And overall, Outlanders plays a bit like a slightly simplified version of World in that it streamlines the more dynamic gameplay. For example, a lot of the emergent world elements, like using a Flashfly to stun a monster, are simple icons that pops up on-screen if you're near. The bigger change, however, is Outlander's two different control schemes: Adventure and Classic. Adventure boils everything down to three buttons – Attack, React, and Burst – automatically and intuitively altering each of these buttons based on the situation. As examples, the Bowgun will swap ammo based on what's most effective in the moment, or the react button might turn into a guard instead of a dodge. Classic control mode gives you more fine-tuned control with more dedicated buttons in the vein of a typical Monster Hunter experience. It works fine on a touchscreen, perhaps even a bit better than I was expecting. But if you opt to use touch controls, I'd heavily recommend the Adventure control scheme, simply because Classic is a lot to juggle without a gamepad-style attachment or acces

sources.title: Capcom quietly updates the Monster Hunter Wilds beta listing on Steam, indicating a possible expansion playtest
sources.text: We might get an early taste of Ascendance before long. Capcom still hasn't announced a release date for Monster Hunter Wilds : Ascendance, the Sunbreak-scale DLC that was revealed in February , but it seems like we might be getting a chance to sample the expansion before too long. A recent Steam listing update has provided a strong reason to suspect that there'll be a public beta for Ascendance available ahead of its launch in 2027. As SteamDB changelogs show, the Steam app entry for Monster Hunter Wilds' 2024 public beta was quietly updated early this morning to change the app's name from "Monster Hunter Wilds Beta test" to "Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance Beta test." Similarly, the listing's visual assets were updated to feature key art of a hunter facing an Arateka, one of the new monsters being introduced in the expansion. And sure enough, while the Wilds beta was removed from player libraries after it ended, it's possible for users who'd previously played it to confirm its listing changes within the Steam app by viewing their own played games from their Steam profile. I just looked. It says Ascendance right there. As the previous Wilds beta consisted of a repackaged demo build, it's likely that an Ascendance beta would follow suit: I'd expect a similar set of hunts to what in-person attendees were able to get hands-on time with at Tokyo Game Show in September, offering a chance to try out the new Boost Bracer weapon mechanics in Master Rank combat. If a beta does materialize, it'll hopefully be a smoother experience than what beta hunters got in 2024. The early Wilds playtest was the first time PC players encountered the dreaded origami monsters , a symptom of the severe optimization issues that tanked Wilds' reputation for over a year after launch. As for when that beta might be available, we can only speculate—but given that Monster Hunter has made prior appearances at Geoff Keighley productions, a public playtest that accompanies a hypothetical Game Awards trailer makes intuitive sense. But I'm just reading the tea leaves here—Capcom hasn't said a word about when it'll offer its next DLC teaser. Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance is set to launch some time in 2027. sources.title: Monster Hunter Wilds' upcoming Ascendance expansion may be getting a beta, some curious Steam backend updates suggest
sources.text: Monster Hunter Wilds 's first expansion, Ascendance, is set for release sometime next year . But, judging by some very suspect recent changes to the Wilds beta app on Steam, we may be playing some of the new stuff earlier than we thought. On Steam, Capcom quietly updated the Monster Hunter Wilds Beta app to now say Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance Beta test. You can see the change log on SteamDB (via PC Gamer ), which also shows an updated key art - all signs that point towards an impending beta for Ascendance. The beta app is the same one those who played the original Wilds beta had in their library. Though the app was removed following the beta's conclusion, because the two share the same ID, the beta should be visible in users' list of played games under the new name. This could mean players won't need to sign up for the supposed Ascendance beta, seemingly only needing to download the new client. Seeing as Ascendance itself doesn't have a release date, beyond a nebulous 2027 target, it's hard to speculate when Capcom plans to release the beta. Sometime early in 2027 would be a good guess, perhaps alongside a release date announcement. Capcom has shown off Ascendance on multiple occasions, more recently in Sony's September State of Play, where we got to see a number of the expansion's new features . A few days later at Tokyo Game Show, we got a first look at returning Elder Dragon Teostra , which we can hunt in the expansion. Capcom is keen for Ascendance to deliver the level of challenge Monster Hunter is known for, following feedback that the launch version of Wilds simply lacked that expected level of difficulty . While post-launch updates have certainly raised the level of challenge , Ascendance looks to be the next step up.

sources.title: Laid-off Id Software devs form employee-owned studio Hidden Horses
sources.text: Developer is launching a Kickstarter campaign to fund its first project, FPS shooter Danger Pay A group of Id Software developers affected by Xbox's mass layoffs have formed an independent, employee-owned studio called Hidden Horses. The studio includes more than 20 former Id Software developers, artists, and designers, and aims to provide staff with an ownership stake in their work. "We're creating a studio where the developers share in its success and have a commitment to it beyond just another job," said co-founder and executive producer Andrew Willis. "I think that when people have a stake in something’s success, they are more committed to it." Hidden Horses wants to utilise this structure to "empower individual developers while maintaining the focused decision-making necessary to build ambitious games." The developer is launching a Kickstarter campaign to fund its first project, the single-player FPS Danger Pay. Funds will support "the typical things needed to start a business and finance game development, including licenses, hardware, and healthcare." The initial fundraising goal will reflect the timeline and costs of the first project. "What excites me about this particular venture is we're taking the two kinds of risk that I was holding before," co-founder and rendering programmer Regan Carver said in a video documenting the studio's founding . "One was, can we succeed, which was a given because we were an established company. We had money coming in. We were making good stuff. And the other was, does the company care about me? For a while, that was true, and then it stopped." "Whereas with this venture, it's like trading one for the other. We know we all care about each other, but all we have to do now is succeed. I've done the former. It didn't work out. I'm ready to do the latter, being able to do what we want and talk through what our ideas are." In July, approximately 136 Id employees were laid off. The developer maintained it still had " the crew we need to build the games and tech we're known for ," despite concerns about its ability to maintain its proprietary game engines with half a team. "The team today is about the same size we were when making Doom (2016)," the developer said in a statement. "We have always had a flat studio where everyone is a maker, and we will remain true to that philosophy moving forward." "We are focused on supporting each other and the team members impacted. We're going to keep building the great games and tech that have defined us for the past 35 years."

sources.name: GamesRadar
sources.title: Laid off Id Software devs form their own studio and don't hold back in their announcement
sources.text: "It's just wild the talent that they let go" Nothing zaps the joy right out of launch day celebrations like getting laid off alongside half of your team, but that's exactly what happened to dozens of Id Software developers during Microsoft's July 2026 bloodbath (not to be confused with its September 2026 bloodbath ) alongside the release of the Revelations DLC for Doom: The Dark Ages. Amid reports that the studio was gutted down to support studio size , the total confirmed number of laid off employees, per Game Developer , was 136 as of this past July, which current studio leadership has confirmed was about half of the team . That's an absolutely devastating loss of institutional talent, but a group of former Id Software devs has risen from the ashes as new worker-owned studio Hidden Horses. In the studio's announcement documentary, they don't hold back. "It's just wild the talent that they let go. It's just wild that they would attack Id like that the day before we release our DLC. It really felt like an attack," says Hidden Horses co-founder and former Id Software tools programmer John-Michael Quinlan. "It was probably emotionally the worst day of my life," says former Id Software senior technical designer Jordan Turner, who's now co-founder and, fittingly, technical designer at Hidden Horses. "I don't think I've cried that much in my entire life." "I did not see it coming at the time that I was told," says former Id Software programmer, now Hidden Horses rendering programmer, Regan Carver. "I just told my wife, 'well that was not a fun conversation.' She thought I was joking at first, and then she realized I wasn't. I was in shock, but she was in tears. "I usually spend the release days scouring social media looking for all the good news. It drives up my morale ... I'm always excited to see people receiving our stuff well and knowing I was a small part of it, so that was gone." Amid a period of historic tumult in the gaming industry, it's easy to become desensitized by news of another mass layoff, but hearing from the workers themselves in this way really underscores the immense human toll of corporate downsizing. Former Id Software AI engineering lead Daniel Young says the hardest part about being laid off was losing friends he'd worked with for years. "It hit me pretty hard. I think that was the biggest thing was the people that I was gonna be leaving behind. I hate to say it's like a death in the family, but it's almost like that's what it felt like," says Young. Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more "Personally the biggest thing was that I'm trying to help my kids through college," says Todd Boyce, former Id Software lead VFX artist and Hidden Horses technical artist. "I have two kids in college right now, and that is really expensive. That's probably the thing that hurts me the most is the possibility of them being financially stressed because of something that wasn't even in their control, and for a layoff that honestly didn't need to happen." Hidden Horses is a small studio of 19 developers according to this announcement video, and its Kickstarter describes its debut title, Danger Pay , as "a single player FPS based around a deadly gameshow with high-octane action and gameplay focused design." Meanwhile, Hidden Horses producer Andrew Willis says players can expect "absolutely stellar out-of-this-world fun gameplay, amazing and super cohesive and stylistic visuals, and really optimized gameplay on the technical side." Technical designer Tim Locke says one key difference between working at a corporate-owned studio like Id and now Hidden Horses is creative freedom. "Being able to do what we want and talk through, like, what are our ideas, like, which ones resonate with the most people and how do we move forward with that. That's really the difference, and it has been different so far. It's been great." Echoing that sentiment, Hidden Horses lighting artist Tyler DeLisle says "the people that were let go at Id ... we were all, none of us were slackers. We were all best of the best, top of our game, so now that we're all given this opportunity to come together and keep doing what we love to do, but kind of untethered and more collaborative, I think we can really put out something special." "If even a small measure of those games that we've worked on in the industry, for me over the past 20 years, is able to be distilled down into a game for our fans, I think they're gonna get something really special," says Quinlan. "And I think you only have to look at the pedigree of the people involved to know that we can do something really special here." Inside Xbox, "the only concrete thing they have communicated is they want higher profits, and they want it now," says id Software employee After earning an English degree from ASU, I worked as a corporate copy editor while freelancing for places like SFX Magazine, Screen Rant, Game Revolution, and MMORPG on the side. I got my big break here in 2019 with a freelance news gig, and I was hired on as GamesRadar's west coast Staff Writer in 2021. That means I'm responsible for managing the site's western regional executive branch, AKA my home office, and writing about whatever horror game I'm too afraid to finish. sources.text: Hidden Horses, co-founded by "approximately 20" former id devs, is planning a Kickstarter campaign to help fund its first project. As part of its July 2026 wave of Xbox job cuts, Microsoft laid off a reported 136 developers from id Software, a studio whose name is synonymous with expertise in shooter design and engineering. Today, "approximately 20" of those former id developers announced the formation of Hidden Horses, an employee-owned game studio boasting "over 250 collective years" of game dev experience between its co-founders. "This team has spent years building games together, and we realized that what made that experience special wasn't just the projects we worked on; it was the people we worked with," Hidden Horses engine programmer and co-founder Dustin Land said in a press release . "Hidden Horses is an opportunity to keep that team together, build something of our own, and create the kind of old school shooters that we think people want more of." On its website , the studio says it was formed as a democratically governed, developer-owned company so it can prioritize "long-term health over short-term growth, longevity over quarterly returns, and innovative gameplay over shady monetization"—for the sake of its games, and the studio staff creating them. "We're creating a studio where the developers share in its success and have a commitment to it beyond just another job," said co-founder and executive producer Andrew Willis, "I think that when people have a stake in something’s success, they are more committed to it.” The studio is planning to launch a Kickstarter campaign to support the development of its first planned game: a singleplayer arena shooter called Danger Pay, in which players will participate in a televised ultraviolent game show inspired by works like The Running Man (the 1987 movie, not the 2025 one) and 1990's Smash TV—a game that, I've just now learned, got a novella adaptation in 1992 . So. Now I get to have that knowledge bouncing around. "We've had the privilege of spending our careers making games for incredible communities of players," said Johnmichael Quinlin, studio co-founder and tools programmer. "Now we have the chance to build something new together, and we're excited to invite those players along for the journey from the very beginning." If you want to stay posted on what Hidden Horses is up to, you can follow the studio on its Bluesky account . sources.title: A group of developers laid off from id Software have formed new studio Hidden Horses
sources.text: The studio is Kickstarting its first game, an FPS called Danger Pay A team of developers who were recently laid off from id Software have formed a new studio, and plan to make a new FPS. Hidden Horses is an employee-owned studio consisting of more than 20 former id Software staff, and aims to “pursue fun and creativity in our games, unencumbered by short-term thinking or chasing market trends”. “As a group of developers who’ve dedicated their careers to making games, we believe this structure allows us to create the kind of company that values long-term health over short-term growth, longevity over quarterly returns, and innovative gameplay over shady monetization,” a statement from the studio reads. The studio has launched a short documentary video explaining how they were all laid off from id Software, how the layoffs affected them, and how they got together to form Hidden Horses. “Okay, you’ve got all these people that do this amazing thing at a high level, that really cannot be replicated, and they’re all out of a job now,” producer Andrew Willis said in the video. “You have all these people on the consumer side that love the games, want more of it, and want more of it than has even been produced in the past. “So, if the money’s out there to buy the stuff that we make, and the people who make that stuff are now free to make more of it, I just thought we should, we could do this. The demand is there, the supply side is there. There’s no reason that we can’t put a company together to continue this on. “Especially as I saw the [ Doom: The Dark Ages ] Revelations DLC critical reviews and player reviews roll in, of just loving it, a lot of them saying it’s the best entry in the whole Doom trilogy from 2016 on, I just became more and more convinced if we put together a company full of these veterans that hold all this immense institutional knowledge, I think the fans would want to buy what they would have to make.” The new studio has turned to Kickstarter in an attempt to get funding for its first game, a first-person shooter called Danger Pay set in a deadly gameshow, with inspiration taken from The Running Man and Smash TV. “Unlike a lot of potential startups, having a team that has already worked together for a decade, you already have those connections,” technical artist Todd Boyce said in the video. “You already all know what each other’s capabilities are. and you already know how to make a game together. To put together a team like the team that this tragedy has kind of spurned, is almost a one in a million opportunity that just doesn’t happen. “Having the ability to inject your own creativity into a project gives you so much more ownership. And this is an opportunity for an entire team to do that on a new project of their own creation. And that is the most exciting thing I could possibly imagine.”
